items.prompt: What causes water inside the container to cool?
options: The outer surface prevents water from changing state
Evaporation removes energy from the container and water
A sealed outer coating keeps warm air away from the stored water
Heat passes into the clay because the material stays colder than the surrounding air
items.explanation: Evaporation carries away energy.
items.title: Cooling water with clay
items.passage:
An unglazed clay container can keep water cooler than the surrounding air under suitable conditions. Its usefulness does not depend on clay being a cold material. Instead, tiny connected spaces in the clay allow a little water to reach the outer surface. When that water evaporates, it takes energy from the container and the remaining water, lowering their temperature.
The process works better when the air can receive more water vapor. Dry air and moving air generally support evaporation, whereas humid, still air can limit it. Consequently, the same container may be effective in one climate and less useful in another. A glazed coating also changes its performance: by sealing the surface, the coating reduces the movement of water through the clay.
There is a trade-off between cooling and water conservation. The cooling effect requires some water to leave the container as vapor, so it is not a way to lower temperature without any loss. The amount lost must be considered when water is scarce.
This example illustrates why understanding a traditional technology requires attention to its environment. Its performance emerges from an interaction among the container, the liquid, and the surrounding air, rather than from a special property of the container considered alone.

items.prompt: What does the author mainly emphasize?
options: Toll records are the most reliable way to reconstruct every use of a bridge
Maintaining a bridge involved continuing social arrangements
Physical remains are less informative than written accounts
A bridge’s initial source of funding determined how it would later be maintained
items.explanation: The passage treats bridge operation as an ongoing responsibility.
items.title: Reading a bridge’s financial records
items.passage:
A historic bridge can reveal the materials and techniques used by its builders. Financial records associated with the bridge can reveal a different kind of structure: the arrangements that kept it in operation. A bridge might have been paid for initially by a wealthy donor, yet depended afterward on small, repeated contributions from people who used it.
Toll records, for example, may distinguish charges for pedestrians, carts, and animals. These differences can help historians identify which activities supported maintenance. However, the records do not provide a complete count of movement. Some travelers may have been exempt, and certain payments may never have been entered. Treating the surviving totals as a precise picture of all traffic would therefore be misleading.
Repair accounts add another perspective. A large expense following a flood may show how a community responded to sudden damage, while modest regular payments can suggest a routine of preventive care. Neither pattern alone establishes whether the bridge was generally reliable; the evidence must be considered alongside other records and the physical remains.
Studying these sources together shifts attention from a bridge as a single achievement to a bridge as an ongoing responsibility. Construction created a crossing, but repeated decisions about money, labor, and access helped preserve it for later users.

items.prompt: Why is a comparison group useful?
options: It ensures that all participants have identical backgrounds
It guarantees that an intervention produces improvement
It makes repeated assessment unnecessary
It helps estimate what would happen without an intervention
items.explanation: A comparison supports investigation of alternative causes.
items.title: The value of a comparison group
items.passage:
A change that follows an intervention is not necessarily caused by it. Students may improve after attending a workshop, for instance, because the workshop helped them, because they gained experience elsewhere, or because they were already improving. A comparison group offers one way to investigate these possibilities.
The purpose of such a group is not to demonstrate that participants are identical in every respect. Rather, it is to provide a reasonable picture of what might have happened without the intervention. If both groups take the same assessment at similar times, an improvement shared by both may reflect a common influence rather than the workshop itself.
How the groups are formed matters. Students who volunteer for extra instruction may already be more motivated than those who do not. Comparing those groups without considering this difference could exaggerate the workshop’s effect. Random assignment, when appropriate and feasible, reduces the likelihood that such preexisting differences systematically favor one group.
Even a carefully designed comparison does not answer every question. A workshop may help one kind of learner more than another, or produce benefits that a short assessment does not capture. The strongest conclusion is therefore usually specific: it describes an observed difference under stated conditions, rather than announcing that an intervention works equally well for everyone.

items.prompt: Why could comparing volunteers with nonvolunteers be misleading?

items.prompt: What problem is the speaker discussing?
options: Sampling is useful only when every site is accessible
Convenient sampling locations may not represent the area studied
River conditions are identical near every bridge
Repeated measurements always produce contradictory results
items.explanation: The talk addresses location bias in sampling.
items.title: Sampling a river fairly

stimulus.title: Sampling a river fairly
stimulus.script:
Imagine that you want to describe water conditions along a river. The easiest sampling point is beside a road, where you can reach the bank safely. It would be tempting to return there every time. Those samples might tell you a great deal about that location, but they wouldn’t necessarily represent the whole river.
Conditions can change near a tributary, a town, or a slow-moving stretch. If all the accessible sites share one feature, such as being beside bridges, then a collection of many samples can still overlook important differences. Increasing the number of measurements doesn’t automatically solve a problem in where those measurements are taken.
A better plan begins with the question. If you’re investigating a change along the river, you need locations that can reveal that change. You might include several types of site and record why each was chosen. Practical limitations still matter; no one should enter an unsafe area merely to make a map look evenly covered.
The aim is not a perfect pattern of dots. It’s a defensible relationship between the samples and the conclusion. When some parts of the river cannot be sampled, stating that limitation helps readers understand what the evidence can and cannot support.

items.prompt: Why may adding more samples fail to solve the problem?
options: The additional samples may share the same location bias
A larger sample prevents comparisons between sites
The river will stop changing after repeated visits
The measuring equipment becomes less reliable with each use
items.explanation: More samples from similarly selected sites can still omit key conditions.

items.prompt: What is the main topic?
options: Why written stories should avoid familiar phrases
The roles of repetition and variation in oral storytelling
How a recording prevents changes in a performance
Why audiences cannot remember long spoken stories
items.explanation: The talk treats repeated frameworks and adaptable performances.
items.title: Remembering a story’s repeated phrases

stimulus.title: Remembering a story’s repeated phrases
stimulus.script:
A long story told aloud may contain phrases that return at important moments. To a reader, the repetition might seem unnecessary. To a storyteller and a listening audience, however, it can provide structure. A familiar phrase signals where the story has reached and what kind of event may follow.
Repeated language can also support memory. The storyteller doesn’t have to create every sentence from the beginning while speaking. A recurring description or introduction offers a stable pattern into which a new action can fit. This doesn’t mean that every performance is identical. Details may change with the occasion, the audience, or the time available.
Think of a repeated phrase as a framework rather than a recording played back word for word. The framework can remain recognizable while allowing variation. For listeners, that combination can make a long performance easier to follow: familiar elements provide orientation, while changing elements sustain interest.
When researchers compare spoken versions of a story, therefore, differences are not always signs of poor memory. Some variation may be part of the practice itself. The interesting question is how performers combine stability and change, keeping enough shared structure for recognition while shaping a particular telling for the people who are present.

items.prompt: How can a recurring phrase help a storyteller?
options: It requires the performer to avoid changing any words
It supplies a reusable structure during performance
It ensures that every event is described in full detail
It removes the need to respond to the audience
items.explanation: Recurring language reduces the need to formulate everything anew.

items.prompt: What misunderstanding does the talk address?
options: Believing that lamps can produce both heat and light
Recognizing that a complete path is needed
Confusing energy transfer with charge being used up
Assuming that a switch can break a circuit
items.explanation: The speaker explicitly distinguishes energy transfer from loss of charge.
items.title: A battery in an electrical circuit

stimulus.title: A battery in an electrical circuit
stimulus.script:
A battery is often described as a container of electricity. That image is convenient, but it can make some aspects of a circuit confusing. A more useful starting point is that the battery provides a difference that can drive charge around a complete conducting path. If the path is broken, the ordinary circuit no longer carries a continuous current.
Consider a simple lamp connected to a battery through a switch. Closing the switch completes the path, and energy is transferred to the lamp, where some becomes light and some becomes heat. The charge itself is not simply used up as it passes through the lamp. Confusing the transfer of energy with the disappearance of charge leads to mistaken predictions about what happens in other parts of the circuit.
Models and analogies can help, provided that we keep their limits in view. Comparing a circuit to water moving around a loop can suggest why a continuous path matters. But not every feature of water in a pipe has an exact electrical counterpart.
The purpose of a model is to support a particular line of reasoning. When it begins to suggest the wrong answer, we need to refine it rather than insist that the real system behave exactly like the familiar example.

items.prompt: What does closing the switch do in the example?
options: Replace the battery’s stored materials
Complete the conducting path
Stop energy from reaching the lamp
Remove charge from the other wires
items.explanation: The closed switch completes the loop.

stimulus.title: A battery in an electrical circuit
stimulus.script:
A battery is often described as a container of electricity. That image is convenient, but it can make some aspects of a circuit confusing. A more useful starting point is that the battery provides a difference that can drive charge around a complete conducting path. If the path is broken, the ordinary circuit no longer carries a continuous current.
Consider a simple lamp connected to a battery through a switch. Closing the switch completes the path, and energy is transferred to the lamp, where some becomes light and some becomes heat. The charge itself is not simply used up as it passes through the lamp. Confusing the transfer of energy with the disappearance of charge leads to mistaken predictions about what happens in other parts of the circuit.
Models and analogies can help, provided that we keep their limits in view. Comparing a circuit to water moving around a loop can suggest why a continuous path matters. But not every feature of water in a pipe has an exact electrical counterpart.
The purpose of a model is to support a particular line of reasoning. When it begins to suggest the wrong answer, we need to refine it rather than insist that the real system behave exactly like the familiar example.

items.prompt: What does the speaker suggest doing when a model misleads?
options: Revise the model’s use or limits
Reject the observations of the real system
Apply the model more literally to every situation
Avoid using any familiar examples in explanation
items.explanation: A model should be refined when its implications become unhelpful.

items.title: Write an Email
items.subject: Helping with the residence welcome event
items.scenario: You agreed to help visitors find their way around at a residence welcome event. A change to your class schedule means you cannot be present for the first hour. You still want to contribute, and you know some preparation work is needed before the event. Write to Alex.
points: Explain the schedule conflict and state when you can attend.
Suggest how you could help before or during the event.
Ask Alex to confirm which arrangement would be most useful.

items.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
items.question: A city is creating information for visitors. It can invest in an interactive phone service or in more signs and printed maps around the city. Which investment would be more valuable? Support your view, considering how different visitors might use the information.
students: A phone service would be better because information can be updated immediately. It could also suggest routes based on a visitor’s interests. Printed maps may be out of date before they are distributed.

I prefer better signs and maps. They work without a charged phone or internet connection. Clear information in the environment also lets people look around and talk to each other rather than constantly checking a screen.
